description: Kestro Aerospace is the space initiative of Kestro Games/Interactive, an independent studio building large-scale real-time simulations. We are based in Aachen (RWTH) and love turning complex physics and real data into experiences anyone can understand. For Space Apps 2026 we are taking on the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge. Our core skills: simulation, interactive 3D visualization. The team is set for now, but feel free to reach out and say hi!
summary: At the lunar south pole the Sun stays within a few degrees of the horizon, so a ridge a few hundred metres away can decide whether a lander has power. Lunar Site Navigator compares landing sites and dates on one screen. For any point on the Moon it computes the 360° terrain horizon from NASA LOLA elevation data and the positions of the Sun and the Earth with NASA SPICE, and reports when each is visible, which piece of terrain blocks it, how many hours that costs, and how far a landing date can slip. At the polar sites every event time carries an uncertainty band. The code and every result are open; the directions, smooth-sphere event times and eclipse contacts are checked against independent sources, the long-term illumination shares against NASA's illumination maps computed from the same LOLA data, and the one check that failed is shown too.
details:
Try it: https://littiary.github.io/lunar-site-navigator/

What it does

- Compares two sites side by side at a chosen time: Sun and Earth visible or hidden, and the time until each rises or sets.

- Shows why: the stretch of terrain that hides the Sun, its distance and direction, and the hours of sunlight it costs.

- Shows when: a 24-month calendar of illumination and Earth visibility for each site, the landing windows that meet a stated requirement, and how many days a planned landing can slip.

- Shows how sure: at the seven polar sites, and for a new coordinate by default, each rise and set time has a band that follows from a stated two-sigma height error of the terrain model. The 13 sites on the 118 m model have none, because no height error has been measured for that model.

- Shows what to change: the effect of raising a mast and, at the three project sites, of landing elsewhere inside a 100 m landing circle.

- Works for any coordinate on the Moon. Twenty sites are prepared, from Apollo 11 to a point in an Artemis III candidate region; a new coordinate is computed in 10 to 20 seconds for a 30-day window on a laptop.

Who it is for and why it matters

Mission and science teams choosing between south-polar landing sites need more than an average illumination map: they need to know when a site has sunlight and a line to Earth, what blocks it, how sure that time is, and what happens when the schedule slips. Lunar Site Navigator answers these questions for two sites at once, on one timeline, and keeps every result open so that students, educators and other teams can reuse it.

How it works

One science core in Python computes everything and writes versioned result packages with checksums. The web view and the Unreal Engine planner only read those packages; neither computes a science result. The horizon is traced on the true sphere out to 300 km, with the Sun treated as a disc so that partial sunrise is included. Terrain is NASA's LOLA 5 m site models at two of our three project sites (at Malapert the 5 m model did not meet our seam check, so the 20 m product is used), the LOLA 20 m and 60 m polar products near the poles, and SLDEM2015 (LOLA merged with Kaguya Terrain Camera data) at 118 m elsewhere. The Sun and Earth directions come from NASA SPICE with the DE440 ephemeris.

Why the numbers can be trusted

For every comparison with an outside source, the pass criterion was committed before the comparison was run; the git history shows the order. Two of the comparisons below, the Apollo angles and the Blue Ghost eclipse, were not blind, because earlier research had already compared some of the published values; the card says so. The validation card in the repository has 32 checks, among them:

- Directions of the Sun and Earth against JPL Horizons, 95,676 rows: within 0.005 arcseconds computed directly, and within 0.1 arcseconds through the direction table the packages use.

- Sunrise and sunset on a smooth sphere against the Horizons rise and set tables: agreement to the one-minute steps of the reference (largest difference 57 s).

- Sun and Earth angles at six Apollo landings, 48 published values: within 0.047°.

- The March 2025 eclipse that Blue Ghost saw from the lunar surface: our contact times agree with the times Firefly predicted for its site within 0.83 minutes.

- Long-term sunlight and Earth-visibility shares against NASA's published LOLA illumination maps of the south pole.

One of the 32 checks did not meet its own criterion: a comparison with an LRO camera image reached 89.6 % against a required 90 %. It stays on the card with the reason.

Separate acceptance checks of the terrain models add: the global models agree within 7 m in height with the five Apollo and Lunokhod laser retroreflectors, and against 192 catalogued craters the 20 m polar model shows no systematic shift above 100 m (estimate 32 m, rotation −0.013°); that catalogue is itself tied to LOLA. Event times on real terrain have no independent reference, and the card says so.

What we learned

At the Shackleton rim, between 14 November and 14 December 2026, a lander with a sensor at 2 m loses about 52 of 720 hours of sunlight to terrain only 0.3 to 0.7 km away. On the 20 m model the hour of the Sun's return is uncertain by 74 hours; with the 5 m site model, by 1.8 hours. At this site, near terrain, not the distant mountains, sets how well the landing can be planned. While checking the data we also documented three discrepancies in public products; the notes are in the repository.

What makes it different

Two sites on one timeline instead of one map at a time; the cause of every loss of sunlight, with its distance and its cost in hours; an uncertainty band on event times that follows from the terrain's height error; and one set of checksummed result packages that drives both a browser view and a real-time Unreal Engine planner.

Limits

Outside the polar products the terrain is 118 m per pixel, so relief narrower than about 240 m is not resolved, and those sites carry no uncertainty band. The only independent height check is the five retroreflectors, and two LROC images test lit and shadowed ground (one agrees, one fails). The landing requirement shown is an example chosen by the team, not a mission requirement.

Built with

Python, NumPy, SpiceyPy (NAIF CSPICE), React, three.js, Unreal Engine 5.8, Blender. More than 600 automated tests. python scripts/bootstrap.py --test sets up a fresh clone and runs them against the committed results.
dataRefs: LRO LOLA gridded elevation models (LDEM 20 m, 60 m, global)
LOLA 5 m site elevation models of the lunar south pole (PGDA 78)
SLDEM2015: LOLA and Kaguya Terrain Camera elevation model (PGDA 54)
LOLA illumination maps of the south pole (PGDA 69)
NASA/JPL NAIF SPICE kernels (DE440, lunar frames, DSN stations)
LROC NAC image M146846913L (lit and shadowed ground check)
NASA SVS CGI Moon Kit (LROC colour map of the Moon globe)
NASA Blue Marble (Earth disc in the 3-D views)
Apollo Lunar Surface Journal (Apollo Sun and Earth angles)
NASA SP-4029 Apollo by the Numbers (landing times)
